# Discussion {#discussion}

\ChapFrame[Discussion][bhtgray]

This chapter consits of the main sections as follows:

Section \@ref(answer-research-questions) interprets the results in relation to our research questions and hypotheses, compares them with previous work, and highlights any surprising or unexpected outcomes.

Section \@ref(error-analysis) contains our error analysis and discusses interesting findings under a researchers perspective.

Section \@ref(general-performance) discusses practical implications and limitations for the planned \acr{HITL} application, as derived from the error analysis. The results are interpreted from an engineering perspective, focusing on how the findings inform the design and implementation of the application.

Subsequent, Section \@ref(not-covered) describes, what we have neither investigated nor implemented in this thesis. Section \@ref(outlook-implementation) gives an outlook on the challenges for implementing the system at \acr{RHvB}. Finally, ethical and practical consideration are presented in Section \@ref(ethics).

## Research questions {#answer-research-questions}

### Page identification

We posed the following research question and hypotheses for the page identification task:

```{r, include=knitr::is_html_output(), results='asis', echo=FALSE}
cat("<ol class='rs-questions' style='--counter: 1;'><li>How can we use LLMs effectively to locate specific information in a financial report?</li></ol>")
```

\begin{enumerate}[label={\textbf{Q\theenumi}}]
  \item How can we use LLMs effectively to locate specific information in a financial report?
\end{enumerate}

**H1.1:** \acr{LLM}s can be used to locate specific information in a financial report, achieving a high F1 score.

**H1.2:** \acr{LLM}s can be combined with other approaches to reduce the energy consumption, without lowering the systems recall.

::: paragraph-start
##### Results

The page identification task is solved by the \acr{LLM} with higher F1 scores than the human reference F1 score for every target class. It is solved perfectly for the documents of our sample for predicting the class **Aktiva**. The multi-class classification with Llama 4 Scout is best for classifying **Aktiva** and **Passiva** tables. The binary classification with Ministral works best for classifying **GuV** tables.
:::

The prompting strategy *n_rag_examples* often yields best results, especially if \acr{icexs} are used. Section \@ref(same-company-evaluation) is discussing this finding for both tasks.

The term frequency approach reaches a top k recall of 1.0 for a small $k = 5$. It runs 100 times faster than the \acr{LLM} approach and reduces the average number of pages to classify by 92.6 %. We discuss how to combine the two approaches in Section \@ref(efficency-discussion).

::: paragraph-start
##### Interpretations

Both of our hypotheses find support. Thus, we see our research question answered with the following statement: It is possible to locate specific information in a financial report using \acr{LLM}s and it can be done more efficient if a term frequency based approach is used for page range refinement in advance.
:::

::: paragraph-start
##### Comparison with previous work

We are able to narrow down the page range to five pages without using a \acr{LLM}. With the \acr{LLM} we are guaranteed, to find the correct pages within a range of two pages. Most of the time, the page, ranked highest in the confidence score ranking, is the correct one. @liExtractingFinancialData2023 do not present a concrete number of pages, they have to process after page refinement.
:::

The \acr{TOC} does not work as well as expected. @liExtractingFinancialData2023 do not report any issues or a low recall value for their \acr{TOC} based approach. Thus, we assumed to find a recall value close to 1.0 for the \acr{TOC} based approach, too. Instead we find a recall of 0.27. We discuss differences in the two approaches in Section \@ref(toc-discussion).

::: paragraph-start
##### Unexpected results

We are surprised by the strong performance of Ministral-8B. It performs better, than other models of the Mistral family, that have been released more recent and have a larger parameter count. It shows one of the strongest performances with the *zero_shot* and *law_context*, too.
:::

We are also positive surprised of the strong performance of the recently released members of the Qwen3 family. The older Qwen3 models could not handle the classification tasks at all — with or without thinking mode[^06_discussion-1] — while the models of Qwen2.5 performed well. We identified the implementation of sparse \acr{MoE} layers to be an architectural difference between the more recent and older Qwen3 models.

[^06_discussion-1]: The Qwen3 models support two operating modes: A thining mode and a non-thinking mode. The thinking mode should yield better answers in complex tasks and the additional amount of processing can be controlled by setting a thinking budget [@qwenteamQwen3ThinkDeeper2025]. This thinking budget can be seen as the amount of tokens used for a step wise solution.

But we assume the difference in the perfromance is caused by a different fine-tuning process. While the original released models already claimed to deliver "groundbreaking advancements in [...] instruction-following" [@QwenQwen34BHugging2025], we now find a newer version of the Qwen3-4B model that explicitly is tagged as Qwen3-4B-Instruction. It would be interesting, to add this model to the benchmark in future work.

::: paragraph-start
##### Conclusion

In summary, our findings demonstrate that LLMs are highly effective for page identification in financial reports, consistently outperforming human benchmarks and traditional rule-based methods. The combination of LLMs with term frequency-based approaches further enhances efficiency, enabling rapid narrowing of candidate pages while maintaining high recall.
:::

Model selection and prompting strategies play a significant role in optimizing performance, with in-context learning using relevant examples yielding the best results. These insights provide a strong foundation for developing robust, scalable solutions for automated document analysis in audit and regulatory contexts.

### Information extraction

We posed the following research question for the information extraction task:

```{r, include=knitr::is_html_output(), results='asis', echo=FALSE}
cat("<ol class='rs-questions' style='--counter: 2;'><li>How can we use LLMs effectively to extract this information from the document?</li></ol>")
```

\begin{enumerate}[label={\textbf{Q\theenumi}}]
  \setcounter{enumi}{1}
  \item How can we use LLMs effectively to extract this information from the document?
\end{enumerate}

We will start discussing the hypotheses group **H2.1** in Section \@ref(extraction-performace-hypotheses-evaluation), before we will look at the hypotheses group **H2.2** in Section \@ref(extraction-performace-predictor-hypotheses-evaluation). The hypotheses of group **H2.1** are:

**H2.1a:** \acr{LLM}s can be used to correctly extract multiple numeric values from the assets table.

**H2.1b:** \acr{LLM}s can match row identifiers and place the numeric values in the correct target row.

**H2.1c:** \acr{LLM}s can identify unmatched row identifiers and report, that the value is missing.

#### Core capabilities {#extraction-performace-hypotheses-evaluation}

::: paragraph-start
##### Results

The best performing model, Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct, almost reaches human performance on real **Aktiva** tables, but is much faster. Both measures, percentage of correct numeric predictions (98.0 %) and F1 score (98.1 %), are not perfect yet and could be improved. It achieves perfect results on synthetic tables provided in \acr{HTML} format.
:::

The prompting strategy *n_rag_examples* often works best, especially if \acr{icexs} are used. Section \@ref(same-company-evaluation) is discussing this finding for both tasks.

::: paragraph-start
##### Interpretations

The high percentage of correct extracted numeric values shows that Qwen3-235B is not only able to exactly copy the values and match corresponding row identifiers, but also to perform numeric transformations, respecting the currency units, in many cases. If no numeric transformations are performed, the upper limit for correct numeric extraction is 80.8 %, because 19.2 % of all numeric values have *T€* as currency unit. We discuss this in Section \@ref(numeric-transformation-discussion).
:::

Furthermore, we can see for the extraction from synthetic **Aktiva** tables, that it is possible to achieve perfect results, if the input is well structured and without unknown row identifiers. In analogy to the concept of *garbage in, garbage out*, we could phrase it as *perfect in, perfect out*. Thus, we show that there is no \acr{LLM} approach inherent mechanism, that prevents perfect information extraction of numeric values. We show this in the Appendix \@ref(error-rat-guidance-synthetic).

The high F1 score shows, that Qwen3-235B also is able to identify missing row identifiers and correctly returns *null* instead of hallucinating numeric values. We discuss the matter of label matching further in Section \@ref(unconsistent-label-matching).

Thus, we conclude, that all hypotheses of group **H2.1** get supported and the research question can be partially answered with the following statement: \acr{LLM}s can be used effectively to extract information from the financial reports using in-context learning and a strict schema.

::: paragraph-start
##### Comparison with previous work

@liExtractingFinancialData2023 achieve a perfect extraction result, after refining their approach, extracting a total of 152 data points from 8 \acr{ACFR} reports. Before the prompt refining they find 96.1 % correct extracted datapoints. Applying the refined approach on a more heterogeneous sample of 4_000 county year \acr{ACFR}s, they achieve a performance of 96 % on 80_000 data points.
:::

Thus, our found performance is higher than their initial in-sample and final out-of-sample performance. Since we did not adjust our prompting strategy before the second iteration of the ground truth creation, we argue that our performance should be compared to their out-of-sample performance.

There are some differences in our prompting approaches, that may have a minor influence on the performance. @liExtractingFinancialData2023 include explicit instructions for handling currency units, which we do not for the extraction task with real **Aktiva** tables. But we investigated this with the synthetic and hybrid approach and discuss the findings in Section \@ref(numeric-transformation-discussion).

@liExtractingFinancialData2023 extract three values per \acr{LLM} call, while we expect 10 to 40 numeric and 18 to 38 *null* predictions per call. They explicitly include an instruction on how to handle missing values and do not report any remarkably higher error rates with missing values. Therefore, we can not compare our F1 score with their results.

::: paragraph-start
##### Unexpected results

We did not expect the \acr{LLM} to perform any currency units related numeric transformations, without being explicitly instructed, (how) to do this. But it is plausible, that this pattern can be learned during in-context learning. This is especially true, if the examples are chosen according to vector similarity and if \acr{icexs} can be used. We describe this in more detail in Section \@ref(same-company-evaluation).
:::

::: paragraph-start
##### Conclusion

The results demonstrate that \acr{LLM}s, are highly effective for extracting structured financial information from assets tables, nearly matching human performance while operating significantly faster. They can accurately extract multiple numeric values, correctly match row identifiers, and reliably identify missing entries.
:::

The success of in-context learning, especially when \acr{icexs} are used, highlights the importance of prompt design and relevant context. While perfect extraction is achievable with well-structured synthetic data, real-world performance is limited mainly by input quality and schema consistency.

Compared to previous work, the approach presented here achieves higher performance without extensive prompt refinement, underscoring the robustness of the method. Unexpectedly, \acr{LLM}s can perform currency-related numeric transformations even without explicit instructions, suggesting that in-context learning can capture the underlying patterns.

Overall, these findings confirm that \acr{LLM}s, combined with a strict schema and in-context learning, offer a reliable and scalable solution for automated information extraction in financial reporting.

#### Feature effects {#extraction-performace-predictor-hypotheses-evaluation}

The hypotheses of group **H2.2** are:

**H2.2a:** Model specific features have an effect on the extraction performance.

**H2.2.b:** Prompt strategy specific features have an effect on the extraction performance.

**H2.2c:** Table specific features have an effect on the extraction performance.

::: paragraph-start
##### Results

The features, that show an noticeable importance value most often, are:
:::

1.  *model_family*
2.  *parameter_count*
3.  *method_family*
4.  *n_examples*
5.  *T_in_previous_year*

We can determine an effect direction for the features *parameter_count*, *n_examples* and *T_in_previous_year*. More parameters and more examples are beneficial. The only exception for this is found for the model Llama 4 Maverick. We discuss this case in section \@ref(context-rot). The performance gain gets smaller comparing experiments with three and more provided examples. The prompting strategies *n_random_examples* and *top_n_rag_examples* perform best.

The method specific feature *respect_units* shows meaningful importance for evaluating synthetic tables. Its effect has opposite direction to our assumption. For the hybrid approach it has a small importance, but with an effect direction matching our assumption. We discuss this in the next paragraph.

With the synthetic tables, we also find that \acr{HTML} and Markdown are a *input_format* that yield better results. We show in section \@ref(alternative-input-formats-extraction), that we do not find these benefits for processing real tables from (imperfect) Markdown input.

::: paragraph-start
##### Interpretations

All model and method specific features are meaningful predictors for the information extraction task. Thus, we argue, that **H2.2a** and **H2.2b** find total support. The high importance of the feature *model_family* could be an artifact of Llama 4 Mavericks bad performance with multiple in-context learning examples.
:::

Of all the table characteristics only *T_in_previous_year* shows a higher importance. Thus, we argue, that **H2.2c** only gets support for a one of the features we proposed a (directed) effect for. There are multiple features we proposed to have no effect and where no effect is found. These hypotheses also get supported by our experiments. We assume, that *T_in_year* would get a higher importance too, if the number of tableswith this characteristic in our sample would be higher.

::: paragraph-start
###### Respecting Units

We find effects with opposite directions for the predictor *respect_units* for the information extraction with synthetic tables and the hybrid approach. This is explained by our experimental designs.
:::

The basic experiments with synthetic tables compare the extracted values with untransformed gold standard values. The in-context learning examples demonstrate no numeric transformations, either. The \acr{LLM} just has to copy the digits. Thus, the task is easier, because no numeric transformation is needed.

If the model is instructed to handle currency units, the extracted values are compared with transformed gold standard values. The in-context learning examples do demonstrate this behavior. Thus, the task is harder, because the model has to learn the numeric transformation pattern.

In contrast, the hybrid approach experiments always compare the extracted values with transformed gold standard values. The in-context learning examples demonstrate this behavior, if the model is instructed to handle currency units. The in-context learning examples do not demonstrate this behavior, if the model is not instructed to handle currency units. Thus, the task is easier, if the model is instructed to handle currency units, because it can learn the patterns from the in-context examples.

::: paragraph-start
##### Compare with previous work

@liExtractingFinancialData2023 report, that the most frequent errors for the extraction of values from \acr{ESG} reports are based on incorrectly handled units. This aligns well with our findings of a high importance value for *T_in_previous_year*. Our results also align well with @brownLanguageModelsAre2020 findings, that the performance might not increase much more by adding additional examples after the second one.
:::

::: paragraph-start
##### Limitations

We failed to reflect the *header_span* and *text_around* characteristics, during the creation of the synthetic \acr{HTML} and Markdown tables. Thus, we can not evaluate the propsed interaction effects with *input_format* for those features. But we find no big importance for *header_span* in any experiment.
:::

We also did not include an indicator, if \acr{icexs} are used, as a method related feature. We show, that this matters in section \@ref(same-company-evaluation).

::: paragraph-start
##### Unexpected results

We did not expect to find such a clear example for context rot as we do for Llama 4 Maverick. We are surprised that we do not find the same behavior with Llama 4 Scout. Since it has an even larger context window, we wonder, if we will observe context rot for Llama 4 Scout too, if we increase the number of in-context learning examples proportionally.
:::

::: paragraph-start
##### Recommendations

We recommend to evaluate the hypotheses for the visual table characteristics once more, when more advanced document parsing methods are used, which process visual information. The method for document parsing should be included as a feature in this future evaluation as well.
:::

::: paragraph-start
##### Conclusion

Overall, both model and prompt strategy features noticeably impact extraction performance, with larger models and well-chosen in-context examples yielding the best results. Table-specific features play a smaller but sometimes meaningful role. In contrast to the classification task, we find no model family that performs worse in general.
:::

Importantly, providing at least one or two relevant examples is more beneficial than simply increasing model size. These findings highlight the need for augmented prompt strategies and model selection to optimize \acr{LLM}-based information extraction.

#### Error rate guidance

We posed the following \acr{UX} inspired side research question and hypotheses:

```{r, include=knitr::is_html_output(), results='asis', echo=FALSE}
cat("<ol class='rs-questions' style='--counter: 3;'><li>Can we use additional information from the extraction process to guide the user on which values need to be checked and which can be trusted as they are?</li></ol>")
```

\begin{enumerate}[label={\textbf{Q\theenumi}}]
  \setcounter{enumi}{2}
  \item Can we use additional information from the extraction process to guide the user on which values need to be checked and which can be trusted as they are?
\end{enumerate}

**H3.1:** The confidence score can be used to guide the user on which of the identified pages need to be checked and which can be trusted as they are.

**H3.2:** The confidence score can be used to guide the user on which of the predicted values in the information extraction task need to be checked and which can be trusted as they are.

::: paragraph-start
##### Results

For the page identification task, we find high confidence intervals with (near) zero empirical error rate for well performing models, containing most of the classifications. Ministral-8B shows a wide spread of confidence scores for the page identification task, that can be used to distinguish correct and wrong classifications.
:::

We do not find high confidence intervals with a error rate below 1 % for the information extraction task on real **Aktiva** tables. Explicitly instructing to respect currency units, reduces the empirical error rate (see Appendix \@ref(hybrid-respect-units)). But we can find confidence intervals with zero error rate for the information extraction task on synthetic data.

::: paragraph-start
##### Interpretations

We find support for the hypothesis **H3.1** but not for hypothesis **H3.2**. Thus we answer the research question as follows: The confidence score can be used to guide users attention for the page identification task, but hardly for the information extraction task.
:::

::: paragraph-start
##### Compare with previous work

The classification task can be interpreted as a best-of-N selection task with two or four choices. Here, our simple measure for confidence seems to be sufficient, aligning well with the findings of @kangScalableBestofNSelection2025.
:::

Generating the information extraction response, can be interpreted as multiple chained best-of-N selections tasks. If every digit, the floating point delimiter, and a end-of-sequence token is counted as individual choice, there are 12 possibilities. Choosing, if a number or *null* should be returned is an additional task with $N=2$ that is to solve multiple times in this decision chain. Even though the number of choices is below $N=16$ for each decision, chaining those choices seems to yield a less meaningful measure of confidence.

::: paragraph-start
##### Unexpected results

Most models predict high confidence for all most of their predictions, even for the wrong ones.
:::

::: paragraph-start
##### Conclusion

In summary, confidence scores are a useful tool for guiding user attention in the page identification task, reliably indicating which pages require review. However, for information extraction, confidence scores are less effective, as high confidence does not consistently correlate with correct predictions. This highlights the need for more robust uncertainty measures in extraction tasks to better support user decision-making.
:::

## Error analysis {#error-analysis}

This section provides a detailed evaluation of the noticeable details found during our evaluation of the experiments. The following sections examine classification errors for each method, analyze the challenges of extracting numeric information and discuss the impact of context rot.

Company-specific results and the influence of example selection strategies are presented, followed by a discussion of numeric transformations and the effects of inaccurate text extraction. The chapter also addresses the performance with a guided decoding aproach and the process of ground truth creation. Each Section aims to highlight practical recommendations and areas for future improvement.

### Page identification {#page-identification-error-analysis}

This section is presenting a brief error analysis for the \acr{LLM} and term frequency approach. We discuss errors related to context rot in Section \@ref(context-rot), because they occurred in both tasks.

#### LLM approach

The seven wrong classified pages by Llama Scout 4 all contain a table, that is filling at least half a page containing one column with text and many columns with numeric values. Six out of those seven are classified as **GuV** and one as **Passiva**. The page, classified as **Passiva** contains the term *Passiva*.

From our point of view it would be more plausible, if page 63 of '/pvc/Geschaeftsberichte/Berlinovo/ berlinovo_Finanzbericht_2021.pdf' is classified as **Aktiva**, because there are a lot of similar row identifiers present. The term frequency approach correctly classifies this page as *other* and ranks it on 8th place for **GuV** and **Passiva** and only on 14th place for **Aktiva**. Thus, our intuition what kind of row identifiers are in the table, is not correct.

To prevent those few incorrect classifications, the system may need more examples for pages, that are similar to the target classes but of different type.

#### Term frequency approach {#error-analysis-tf}

Inspecting some of the pages that are ranked high and wrongly classified as **Aktiva** by the term frequency based random forest, we find, that the normalized sum of term occurrences can lead to missclassification. For example, we find a page identified as **Aktiva**, that contains no single table but a long text. The full term count list based on the **Aktiva** term list can be found in the Appendix \@ref(tf-missclassifications).

The term 'Geschäfts' is present 19 times. The term 'Unternehmen' is present 10 times. Those terms are probably present very often all over the document. Thus, they should get less weight. The \acr{BM25} measure is attributing less weight to common terms and includes an saturation term, too. @kongOpenTabAdvancingLarge2024 shows, that \acr{BM25} can be used effectively to identify relevant tables.

Using a boolean indicator, if a the term is present on a page, instead of counting their individual occurrences, could also be a solution.

We also find pages that are missclassified, because they have a high density of floats. An example for a page with high float density that is not containing an **Aktiva** table can be found in Figure \@ref(fig:tf-many-floats) in the appendix.

We formulate our practical recommendations in Section \@ref(tf-practical-recommendation).

### Information extraction

#### General findings

One of the tested \acr{LLM} families[^06_discussion-2] is not able to handle German Umlaute. Thus we replace those characters with their non-umlaut equivalent and adjusted our schema accordingly.

[^06_discussion-2]: We think it Google's gemma models struggel with Umlaute. But we missed to note the exact family's name and had no time to reconstruct this issue.

In general the approach seems not be prone to hallucinations. When we accidentally tried to extract values from a **Passiva** and **GuV** table, no prediction was made, because non of the row identifiers matches our strict schema.

#### Company specific results {#same-company-evaluation}

::: paragraph-start
##### Real tables

Figure \@ref(fig:extraction-qwen235-by-company) shows, the precision and recall values for predicting a missing value and the percentage of correct numeric predictions for Qwen3-235B for each company. The number after the company name, as well as the color of the boxes indicate, how many of the numeric columns have *T€* as currency unit. The crosses indicate the individual scores per document. The teal crosses represent predictions, if \acr{icexs} are used for the *top n rag* prompting strategy. Red ones represent predictions, where this is not the case.
:::

```{r extraction-qwen235-by-company, echo=echo_flag, warning=warning_flag, message=message_flag, out.width="100%", dev=std_dev, fig.cap="Comparing the F1 score for predicting the missingness of a value for OpenAi's LLMs with some Qwen 3 models. The green crosses indicate results where a model has predicted only numeric values even though there have been missing values.", fig.width=8, fig.height=10}

df_real_table_extraction_best_by_company <- df_real_table_extraction %>% 
  filter(str_detect(model, "235B")) %>% 
  filter(n_examples == 5, method_family == "top_n_rag_examples") %>% 
  # group_by(company) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(NA_precision, percentage_correct_numeric, NA_recall))

df_real_table_extraction_best_by_company %>% 
  mutate(columns_with_T_EUR = ordered(n_T_EUR)) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_boxplot(
    aes(y = paste(company, n_T_EUR), x = value, fill = ),
    alpha= .7
    ) +

    aes(y = paste(company, n_T_EUR), x = value, color = same_company),

    ) +
